ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Wilderness and Expedition Medicine Consultation — Robert Falcon Scott

code.originalText: Two-week follow-up with home blood pressure readings, and wilderness and expedition medicine consultation

text.paragraph: Pre-expedition assessment of a 41-year-old naval officer who will lead a long Antarctic expedition sailing in about five months, with a winter in a hut and sledge journeys of several months on foot. Please advise on his fitness and any further testing, the management of a newly raised blood pressure in that setting, nutrition and scurvy prevention, cold injury and altitude precautions, mental health and sleep in isolation, and an evacuation and communication plan. [S]

list.item: Is he fit for a long polar expedition with heavy sledge hauling, and does he need any further cardiac or other testing?
If his blood pressure is confirmed as raised, how and when should it be treated, given cold, dehydration and long marches?
What nutrition plan, including energy and vitamin C, will prevent the scurvy and weight loss of his earlier journey?
What frostbite, hypothermia and altitude precautions and training does the party need?
How should his mental health and sleep be supported in months of isolation and polar light?
What evacuation, communication and medical kit plan is appropriate?

text.paragraph: Mr. Scott, a 41-year-old naval officer, is seen at the request of Dr. Harrow-Mbeki before he leads an Antarctic expedition that sails in about five months. He is well, with no chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, fainting, or exercise limitation, and walks fast every day. Home readings since his intake visit average 138/88 mmHg. He stopped his pipe a week ago on varenicline. On a long sledge journey in his mid-thirties he developed red gums and swelling of the ankles and legs, which improved within days on fresh seal meat and returned when the meat ran short; after the journey he had swollen legs, sore gums and weeks of exhaustion before a full recovery. This expedition will include a voyage south, a winter in a hut with weeks of darkness, and sledge journeys of up to several months hauling loads on foot, partly on a high plateau, with no evacuation possible for much of the year. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Robert Falcon Scott was born on June 6, 1868, at Plymouth, Devon, into a seafaring family, and joined his first Royal Navy ship when he was 13. [D]
He led the Discovery expedition to the Antarctic from 1901 to 1904. [D]

In October 1902, at the Discovery's winter quarters, scurvy was found after a sledge party returned from the western journey; the expedition's surgeon then examined everyone on board and found signs in a good many men, in most only the merest indication, and the outbreak was over by about October 20. Scott arranged to replace part of the sledging pemmican with cooked seal meat. [D]

On the southern sledge journey (November 1902 to February 1903) the party examined gums and legs every Sunday. When one companion developed angry-looking gums in late December 1902, they stopped eating bacon and increased the seal-meat ration, and Scott recorded that the scurvy symptoms lessened. [D]

At a thorough medical examination on the southern journey on January 14, 1903, Scott recorded that he himself had "distinctly red gums, and a very slight swelling in the ankles." Two days later, on a double ration of seal meat, his gums were much cleaner and his leg vastly improved; by the last days of the journey he wrote that their scurvy had been advancing again and that his ankles were considerably swollen. [D]

After the southern party returned to the ship in February 1903, Scott wrote that he had both legs much swollen and very uncomfortable gums, and an extraordinary lassitude, physical and mental, that lasted many weeks before he returned to a normally vigorous condition. [D]

In his account of the Discovery expedition he wrote that scurvy was then believed to be ptomaine poisoning from tainted meat. A modern historian of medicine notes that many British doctors of the time accepted this view and overlooked the experiments of Holst and Frølich on dietary deficiency, so medical advice given to him before his second expedition would probably not have helped him prevent scurvy. [R]
On the southern journey, on December 20, 1902, he wrote that his tobacco supply was so low that he had been trying tea leaves, which were "nothing less than horrid." [D]

After the Discovery expedition the needs of the naval service called him to the command of battleships and to confidential work at the Admiralty, and five years passed before he resumed Antarctic work. In 1908 he married the sculptor Kathleen Bruce; they had one son. [D]

On November 24, 1909, he wrote from the offices of the British Antarctic Expedition at 36 and 38 Victoria Street, London, that the Pole was at the forefront of the campaign for raising funds but that scientific work would not be neglected. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Fitness for a long polar expedition. He is fit to take part, including in long sledge journeys. He has no symptoms and a low ten-year cardiovascular risk, so an exercise test or echocardiogram would add little and is not needed; a graded training program before departure will prepare him better. Dental, hearing and eye checks are worth completing, because none can be fixed in the field. [S]

Stage 1 hypertension (I10). Confirmed by home readings, with no sign of target-organ damage on the tests so far; the urine albumin test is still needed. At his low risk the guideline advises three to six months of lifestyle measures first, which fits his timetable. If the home average stays at or above 130/80 at about three months, an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan is the best choice for the expedition: a thiazide adds to salt and water loss with cold diuresis and long marches, and a beta-blocker can worsen cold extremities and blunt the response to exercise. It should start at least four weeks before departure, so that electrolytes and creatinine can be checked two to four weeks after starting, with written sick-day rules for vomiting, diarrhea and dehydration. [S]

Personal history of scurvy; nutrition for man-hauling (Z86.39). His earlier scurvy came from months without fresh food, and his recovery on seal meat fits vitamin C deficiency. Scurvy can appear after one to three months of very low intake, so a reliable daily source is essential on preserved rations. Man-hauling in extreme cold needs roughly 5,000 to 6,500 kcal a day, more than earlier sledging rations gave, and energy-dense fat is the lightest way to carry it. [S]

Cold injury and altitude. Frostbite and hypothermia are the main environmental threats on the journeys. Prevention, early recognition, and correct field treatment (rewarming only when refreezing can be prevented) matter more than any medicine. The polar plateau is high, and the cold makes its effect on the body greater than its height suggests, so altitude illness is possible on the ascent. [S]

Mental health and sleep in isolation. PHQ-9 3 and GAD-7 4 are minimal. The polar winter, constant daylight on the journeys, crowding, and months of separation from his family are known strains; a plan made now is more useful than a crisis plan later. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Harrow-Mbeki's intake note and results: ECG sinus rhythm without left ventricular hypertrophy; sodium 140, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL (eGFR 107), fasting glucose 92 mg/dL, HbA1c 5.3%, LDL cholesterol 122 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, hemoglobin 15.1 g/dL; PHQ-9 3, GAD-7 4, AUDIT-C 3. Home blood pressure log: 28 readings over seven days, average 138/88 mmHg. No urine albumin result yet. [S]

list.item: No exercise test or echocardiogram; a graded training program with weighted-pack walks and endurance work before departure. [S]

Blood pressure: lifestyle measures now; home readings before each visit; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; if the home average is still 130/80 or higher at about three months, start losartan, at least four weeks before departure, with electrolytes and creatinine in two to four weeks and written sick-day rules; avoid thiazides and beta-blockers. [S]
Stop tobacco completely, with varenicline and counseling, because nicotine narrows skin blood vessels and adds to frostbite risk; no nicotine products in the field. [S]

Nutrition: about 5,000 to 6,500 kcal a day on man-hauling journeys with a high fat share; weigh weekly in the hut; fresh seal meat when available; vitamin C 250 mg daily from tablets packed in every sledging ration when no fresh food is available, well above the recommended 90 mg and far below the 2,000 mg upper limit; a weekly check of gums and legs. [S]

Cold injury: a wilderness first aid course before departure for him and the sledging parties, covering frostbite and hypothermia prevention, rewarming in water at 37 to 39 °C only when refreezing can be prevented, ibuprofen for frostbite, gentle handling and insulation of hypothermic casualties, and casualty packaging in a sledge. [S]
Altitude: gradual ascent to the plateau, with acetazolamide in the medical kit to treat acute mountain sickness. [S]

Mental health and sleep: repeat PHQ-9 and GAD-7 before departure; a fixed routine, bright light in the polar winter and eye masks in constant daylight, a monthly self-check, and a named person in the party to talk to. [S]

Evacuation and communication: a written plan with satellite messaging where it reaches, the seasonal evacuation windows, and a medical kit, medicine supply and medical summary sized for a year without resupply. [S]
Dental examination and cleaning, audiometry, and an eye examination with spare glasses and glacier glasses before departure. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Harrow-Mbeki, who saw him the same day. The plan was explained to Mr. Scott, who agreed with it and was reassured that nothing found so far stops him leading the sledge journeys. [S]
Follow-up: Available for review of the expedition plan before departure and by telemedicine during the expedition when communication allows. [S]
